answer:
HYPOTHESIS (natural-language, data-grounded)

Among black NLSY79 respondents, incarceration (ever_jailed, 1985–1994) is associated with substantially slower wealth accumulation and a higher probability of ending with no positive wealth — and the association is largest for those who were not at the very bottom to begin with. Because the dataset contains no income variable, "income levels" are proxied by baseline (1985) composite wealth, stratified into terciles within the black subsample (T1 ≤ $0; T2 $0–$3,830; T3 > $3,830).

By 1996, within every baseline-wealth stratum, ever-jailed black respondents are worse off than never-jailed peers with the same starting position:
- Lowest tercile (T1, jailed n=76 vs never n=1,240): baseline wealth is effectively zero for both (median $0). By 1996 the jailed group's mean wealth is $6,093 vs $23,274 (gap −$17,181; winsorized −$14,326), and only 22% hold positive wealth vs 45% of the never-jailed. Median differences are masked at $0 by floor effects, so this stratum shows the incarceration association mainly as a halving of the chance of accumulating any wealth.
- Middle tercile (T2, jailed n=39 vs never n=654): starting positions are statistically indistinguishable (medians both $1,400; p=0.85). By 1996 the jailed median falls to $0 while the never-jailed median rises to $7,450 (gap −$7,450); mean gap −$29,393 (winsorized −$28,252). Positive-wealth share: 38% vs 72%. DiD-style mean change 1985→1996: +$10,196 (jailed) vs +$39,587 (never), a gap of −$29,391.
- Highest tercile (T3, jailed n=44 vs never n=960): despite comparable 1985 wealth (medians $11,150 vs $11,900; MWU p=0.99), the jailed group's median wealth drops from $11,150 (1985) to $4,700 (1996) — it does not grow at all — while the never-jailed median rises to $26,750. Median gap −$22,050; DiD mean-change gap −$59,008; positive-wealth share 55% vs 78%. This is the largest relative setback: incarceration is associated with a complete arrest of wealth growth among those who began with meaningful assets.

The gradient is thus U-shaped in relative terms: at the floor (T1) there is little wealth left to lose (a "nothing-to-lose" floor effect compresses level differences but halves the probability of any accumulation), while in the mid and upper terciles the jailed group loses both the level and the growth trajectory — median 1996 wealth is $0 (T2) or $4,700 (T3) versus $7,450 and $26,750 for never-jailed peers, with rank-based tests significant in all strata (MWU p<0.001 for 1990 and 1996 in T2/T3, p<0.001 in T1 for levels despite $0 medians).

Robustness and checks: quartile robustness was run where jailed cell sizes stayed ≥30 (Q1 n=76, Q3 n=42, Q4 n=34); Q2 was skipped (jailed n=7 < 30). Quartiles confirm the pattern (e.g., Q3: 1996 median −$12,000, DiD mean gap −$41,495; Q4: median −$19,075, DiD gap −$58,632). Winsorization at the 99th percentile leaves mean gaps essentially unchanged, and the positive-wealth indicator shows the same ordering. Sex-stratified check: jailing is heavily male-concentrated among black respondents (143/1,465 men vs 16/1,548 women jailed), yet the negative association appears in both sexes (male DiD mean gap 1985→1996 −$39,526; female −$30,529, based on only 16 jailed women), and a sex-demeaned pooled comparison among black respondents yields a 1996 gap of −$42,189 — so the pattern is not a male-only artifact. White reference contrast: the same within-stratum pattern appears among white respondents (e.g., T3 jailed n=13: median falls from $30,000 to $12,200 while never-jailed rises $48,000→$106,000), suggesting incarceration is associated with wealth loss across races; the black–white gap in levels persists at every stratum regardless of jailing.

In short: incarceration is associated with a wealth penalty for black individuals at every baseline wealth/income position, but it is expressed differently across the distribution — near the bottom it manifests as a sharply lower probability of accumulating any positive wealth (22% vs 45% by 1996), while in the middle and especially the top of the baseline distribution it manifests as stagnant or negative wealth growth (medians falling from $1,400→$0 and $11,150→$4,700 respectively), i.e., a complete forfeiture of the wealth accumulation that otherwise-stratified peers achieve.

This is an observational association, not a causal estimate: jailing status covers 1985–1994 (so the 1990 comparison is contemporaneous with the jailing window, not a clean pre/post), the composite's construction and units are undocumented, ~30–41% of wealth values are ≤0 (floor effects), treated cells are small (39–76 per tercile), sex is the only available covariate, and the processed file's zero missingness precludes assessing panel attrition.

payload.hypothesis: Among black NLSY79 respondents, ever having been jailed (1985-1994) is associated with sharply lower wealth by 1996 at every baseline (1985) wealth/income position, but the form of the association varies across the distribution: in the lowest baseline-wealth tercile (<= $0 in 1985; jailed n=76 vs never n=1,240) floor effects compress median differences (both $0), and the penalty appears as a much lower probability of accumulating any positive wealth by 1996 (22% vs 45%; mean gap -$17,181); in the middle tercile ($0-$3,830; n=39 vs 654), starting wealth is identical (median $1,400) yet jailed respondents' median wealth falls to $0 by 1996 vs $7,450 for never-jailed (mean gap -$29,393; DiD-style mean-change gap 1985->1996 of -$29,391); and in the highest tercile (>$3,830; n=44 vs 960), jailed respondents' median wealth does not grow at all, falling from $11,150 (1985) to $4,700 (1996) while never-jailed peers rise from $11,900 to $26,750 (median gap -$22,050; DiD mean-change gap -$59,008). The incarceration-wealth association among black individuals is therefore weakest in absolute wealth terms at the bottom (nothing-to-lose floor effect) and strongest in the middle and upper baseline-wealth strata, where it manifests as stagnant or negative wealth growth and a roughly halved probability of holding positive wealth. No income variable exists in the data, so 'income levels' are proxied by 1985 composite wealth terciles. These are observational associations conditional on baseline wealth, not causal estimates: jailing status spans 1985-1994 (the 1990 comparison is contemporaneous with the window, not a clean pre/post), composite wealth construction/units are undocumented, ~30-41% of wealth values are <=0 (floor effects), treated cells are small (39-76 per tercile), sex is the only covariate (jailed black respondents are overwhelmingly male: 143/1,465 men vs 16/1,548 women; the negative association holds in both sexes), and the processed file's complete absence of missing values precludes assessing panel attrition.
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows; verified race values white/black/'hipanic' [typo of hispanic, reported as observed], ever_jailed clean 0/1, zero missingness; wealth composites heavily right-skewed and zero-inflated with negative values, no top-coding). 2) Because the dataset has no income variable, proxied 'income levels' with baseline (1985) composite wealth, restricted to black respondents (n=3,013, 159 ever-jailed). 3) Stratified black respondents into 1985-wealth terciles (primary) and compared ever-jailed vs never-jailed within each stratum on 1990 and 1996 wealth levels (medians primary, means secondary, n per cell reported) and on within-stratum change 1985->1990 and 1985->1996 (DiD-style: jailed-group change minus never-jailed-group change); 1990 labeled contemporaneous-with-window, 1996 given equal weight as the post-window outcome. 4) Sensitivity: winsorization at 99th percentile, positive-wealth indicator, quartile stratification restricted to strata with jailed n>=30 (Q2 skipped, n=7). 5) Sex-stratified sanity check within the black subsample plus sex-demeaned pooled comparison. 6) Secondary white reference contrast with identical tercile design. Scripts: analysis/nls_incarceration_analysis.py, analysis/did_fix_and_quartiles.py; full printed output in analysis/analysis_output.txt.
